Third Hour
THURD OWR
noun
A rendering of the Jewish reckoning of the daylight hours, counted from sunrise: the “third hour” is roughly nine in the morning, three hours after the day began. The hours of the night were counted likewise, from sunset.

Biblical Definition

The third hour is nine o’clock in the morning by the reckoning of Scripture, which numbered the twelve daylight hours from sunrise. It is not our third hour but the third after dawn, and the modern reader who forgets the difference will misplace every clock in the Gospels. Peter appeals to it on the day of Pentecost, answering the charge of drunkenness: “these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day” (Act 2:15) — too early for wine, and so the tongues of fire must be owned as the promised Spirit and not the fruit of the cup. It is an hour of labour in the Lord’s parable of the vineyard: the householder “went out about the third hour, and saw others standing idle in the marketplace” (Mat 20:3), and hired them into his field — a picture of the free call of grace at every hour of the day. And it is the hour of the crucifixion in Mark’s plain account: “And it was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mar 15:25) — the Lamb of God nailed up at the morning hour of the temple sacrifice. The hours of the night were counted the same way from sunset, as when the chief captain readied his soldiers for Paul “at the third hour of the night” (Act 23:23). So the third hour teaches the reader to keep Scripture’s own clock: nine in the morning, when the Spirit fell, when the labourers were called, and when the Son of God was lifted up.

Webster 1828 Definition

Nine o’clock in the morning by the Jewish reckoning, which counted the twelve daylight hours from sunrise.

expand to see more

THIRD HOUR, the third hour after sunrise; about nine in the morning.

Scripture numbered the twelve hours of daylight from dawn, not from midnight.

The hours of the night were likewise counted from sunset (Act 23:23).

Peter says it is but the third hour, too early for drunkenness (Act 2:15).

It was the third hour when they crucified the Lord (Mar 15:25).

Key Scripture

Act 2:15 — "For these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day."

Mar 15:25 — "And it was the third hour, and they crucified him."

Mat 20:3 — "And he went out about the third hour, and saw others standing idle in the marketplace,"

Act 23:23 — "And he called unto him two centurions, saying, Make ready two hundred soldiers to go to Caesarea, and horsemen threescore and ten, and spearmen two hundred, at the third hour of the night;"

Modern Corruption

Nine in the morning, not our third hour; the word recovers Scripture’s own clock, reckoned from sunrise and sunset.

expand to see more

The honest error to correct is the imported clock. A modern reader hears “the third hour” and thinks of three in the morning or three by his own watch, and so the day of the Gospels comes apart in his hands. Scripture counts the twelve hours of light from sunrise: the third hour is about nine in the forenoon, the sixth is noon, the ninth is three in the afternoon, and the hours of the night run likewise from sunset. Keep that clock and the accounts fall into order — Peter’s crowd is charged with drunkenness at nine in the morning, and he answers that the hour itself refutes them; the labourers are hired through the working day; the darkness at the crucifixion falls from the sixth hour to the ninth, noon to mid-afternoon.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordered day under God. Scripture’s hours are not vague; they are marked, and the marking matters. At the third hour the Holy Ghost was poured out and the Church was born; at the third hour, by Mark’s reckoning, the Lord was crucified; at the third hour the householder went out to call the idle into his vineyard. The hours of prayer were kept — Peter and John went up to the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer (Act 3:1). A people that keeps no hours keeps no watch; the God who appointed the sun to rule the day appointed its hours too, and filled them with His works.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means nine in the morning, the third of the twelve daylight hours counted from sunrise.

expand to see more

Third hour — the third hour after sunrise, about nine in the forenoon.

Scripture counts the twelve hours of daylight from dawn, not from midnight.

The hours of the night were reckoned the same way, from sunset (Act 23:23).

At the third hour the Spirit fell and Peter answered the charge (Act 2:15).

At the third hour, by Mark, the Lord Jesus was crucified (Mar 15:25).

Usage

"The third hour is nine in the morning, not our third hour: Scripture counts from sunrise."

"It is but the third hour, said Peter — too early for wine, so own the Spirit instead."

"It was the third hour, and they crucified him: the Lamb slain at the morning sacrifice."
